headline: Blaine delegates pour into Chicago
summary: With the Republican National Convention about to open, Roosevelt watches more delegates stream into Chicago, and the newcomers lean heavily toward James G. Blaine.

events.detail: Delegates keep arriving in Chicago ahead of the convention, the majority backing Blaine

headline: Fighting Powell Clayton's bid to chair
summary: Roosevelt teams up with his friend Henry Cabot Lodge to block Powell Clayton, a machine politician they consider corrupt, from being named temporary chairman of the convention.

events.detail: Works alongside Lodge to stop Powell Clayton from becoming the convention's temporary chairman

headline: Speaking up for John R. Lynch
summary: On the convention's sunny first day, the New York delegates take the front center rows. Roosevelt rises to back John R. Lynch of Mississippi, a Black Republican, for temporary chairman, and Lynch wins. All day he pushes hard against Blaine.

events.detail: Delegates march to the hall for the opening session; New York sits up front
Speaks in favor of John R. Lynch for temporary chairman; Lynch is elected
Labors without letup to stop Blaine's nomination

headline: Rain and routine at the convention
summary: A damp day in Chicago brings ordinary convention business, while supporters of Senator George F. Edmunds scheme to hold off the nomination.

events.detail: Routine proceedings on the convention floor
Edmunds backers work to push back the nominating vote

headline: Platform read and nominating speeches
summary: Rain falls again as the delegates receive women's suffrage petitions and hear William McKinley present the party platform. Sixteen nominating speeches fill the evening, and the hall doesn't empty until 1:45 in the morning.

events.detail: Petitions for votes for women are presented to the convention
William McKinley reads out the Republican platform
An evening of sixteen speeches putting candidates in nomination
Session finally adjourns after midnight

headline: Blaine wins on the fourth ballot
summary: Voting starts and Blaine gains ground on every roll call. After the third ballot Joseph Foraker moves to recess and Roosevelt leaps up shouting in support, but the motion fails in the uproar. Blaine takes the nomination on the fourth ballot with 541 votes.

events.detail: Balloting opens with Blaine climbing on each count
Roosevelt loudly backs Foraker's recess motion, which is defeated amid chaos
Blaine nominated: 541 to Arthur's 207 and Edmunds's 41

headline: Off to the Badlands after defeat
summary: Beaten at the convention, Roosevelt leaves Chicago and heads west for Dakota, and the papers note his retreat to the wilds.

events.detail: Leaves Chicago bound for the Badlands
Newspapers report that Roosevelt has headed for the woods

headline: A gloomy letter from St. Paul
summary: Traveling west, Roosevelt writes his sister Bamie from St. Paul that the reformers have been crushed, and he judges Blaine the worst choice of anyone the convention weighed.

events.detail: Rides the train west through Minnesota
Writes Bamie about the convention loss and his view of Blaine

letters.topic: The convention defeat and why Blaine was the worst candidate

tr_quotes.text: Our defeat is an overwhelming rout.

headline: Back at the Little Missouri
summary: Roosevelt steps off the train in Medora, where Joe and Sylvane Ferris and Bill Merrifield greet him and talk over the convention at the newspaper office. A St. Paul Pioneer Press interview quotes him saying he will stay with the party ticket.

events.detail: Arrives at Medora; greeted at the depot by the Ferris brothers and Merrifield
Discusses the convention with his partners at the printing office
St. Paul Pioneer Press prints an interview, with a sketch of his looks and manner

tr_quotes.text: Arrived at my cattle ranche ('Chimney Butte Ranche') on the Little Missouri.
I shall bolt the nomination of the Convention by no means.

uncertain: The record says 'The Ferrises', taken to mean Joe and Sylvane Ferris.

headline: Riding out to the Maltese Cross
summary: Roosevelt saddles up and rides from town to his Maltese Cross Ranch.

events.detail: Makes the ride out from town to his ranch

headline: A day at the Maltese Cross
summary: Roosevelt is at his Maltese Cross Ranch; no other activity is recorded.

events.detail: Spends the day at the ranch

headline: 1,000 more cattle for $26,000
summary: Roosevelt signs a second deal with Sylvane Ferris and Bill Merrifield, paying $26,000 for a thousand head of cattle. Back East, his refusal to bolt Blaine has made the news, and New York's Union League Club blackballs him for it.

events.detail: Signs a new contract with his partners for 1,000 cattle at $26,000
Union League Club blackballs him for standing by Blaine

uncertain: The record names only 'Ferris'; Sylvane Ferris was the partner in the cattle contracts.

headline: Fitted for a buckskin suit
summary: Staying at Gregor Lang's, Roosevelt bags a jackrabbit and a curlew with his heavy express rifle and is itching to go after antelope. Mrs. Maddox takes his measurements for a buckskin outfit.

events.detail: Shoots a jackrabbit and a curlew with his .50-caliber express rifle
Mrs. Maddox measures him for a buckskin suit

tr_quotes.text: One jack rabbit, one curlew.
Both killed with double barrelled express rifle, 50 calibre 150 grains of powder.

headline: Two curlew with the rifle
summary: At the Maltese Cross, Roosevelt drops two curlew with his rifle, one in flight, and is pleased with the shooting. Harper's Weekly declares against Blaine.

events.detail: Kills two curlew with a rifle, one on the wing
Harper's Weekly takes a stand against Blaine

tr_quotes.text: Two curlew, one on wing, both with rifle; good shots.

headline: Setting out after antelope
summary: Roosevelt prepares to leave the Maltese Cross on a four-day antelope hunt.

events.detail: Plans a multi-day antelope hunt

tr_quotes.text: Four days hunt after antelope

headline: A badger run down on horseback
summary: Roosevelt spots a badger far from its burrow, gallops up and kills it with his revolver, then watches a cattle roundup.

events.detail: Chases down a badger on the open plains and shoots it with a revolver
Watches a roundup

tr_quotes.text: One badger; found out on plains away from hole, gallopped up to him and killed him with revolver.

headline: Ranching becomes his business
summary: Roosevelt tells Bamie the St. Paul interview was made up, delights in the June weather after thirteen hours on horseback, and says ranching will be his real business. He means to bring Bill Sewall and Wilmot Dow out from Maine. To Lodge he admits he has heard no news since the convention.

events.detail: Writes Bamie disowning the St. Paul interview and describing long days in the saddle
Decides to make cattle ranching his main occupation
Writes Lodge that he knows nothing of events since the convention

letters.topic: Disowns the press interview; his June riding; plan to ranch full time
Cut off from political news since Chicago

tr_quotes.text: I just saw my alledged St. Paul Interview for the first time. It is wholly ficticious.
glorious June
I am absolutely ignorant of what has been said or done since the convention.

headline: A fine buck antelope at full gallop
summary: Riding alone on the prairie, Roosevelt races his pony across the path of a small band of antelope, jumps down and drops a big-horned buck. From a cattleman's shack he writes Lodge asking to see him soon and insisting they cannot bolt the party.

events.detail: Kills a buck antelope after galloping to cut off a running band
Writes Lodge from a cow camp hut about refusing to bolt Blaine

letters.topic: Wants to meet soon; they must not leave the party

tr_quotes.text: 1 buck antelope, fine horns.

A group of buck six or eight feeding together started to run across my path, while I was riding alone on the prairie; I was on a first rate pony, and galloped at full speed diagonall to their course; I leaped off as they passsed within twenty five yards, and have them both barrels, killing a fine buck, shot through both shoulders.
I wish to see you at once.
We can take part in no bolt

uncertain: 'Have them both barrels' in the diary likely means 'gave'; it is left as written.

headline: Out on the antelope hunt
summary: Roosevelt is away hunting; no details survive for the day.

events.detail: Continues his hunt on the plains

headline: Still hunting on the prairie
summary: Another day afield for Roosevelt, with nothing further recorded.

events.detail: Keeps hunting

headline: His best rifle shot yet
summary: Rounding a knoll, Roosevelt sees two antelope watching from far off. He gets down, aims high and breaks one's neck at a measured 300 yards, the longest shot he has ever made. He spends the night in the trees.

events.detail: Kills an antelope at 300 yards, firing offhand
Camps for the night in timber

tr_quotes.text: One antelope.

On riding round a little knoll, I saw two antelope a long distance off, looking at me; I dismounted and fired off hand, with careful aim, holding a foot over him, and breaking his neck near the shoulder. By actual measurement the distance was three hundred yards; the best shot I ever made with the rifle.
in timber

headline: Return to the Maltese Cross
summary: Roosevelt comes back to the Maltese Cross Ranch from his hunting trip.

events.detail: Gets back to the ranch after hunting

headline: Playing frontier hunter in earnest
summary: After shooting two plover for the cook pot, Roosevelt tells Bamie he has spent a week alone on the plains, sleeping out under the sky, and has two antelope and a deer to show for it.

events.detail: Shoots two field plover with a rifle for food
Writes Bamie about solo nights on the prairie and his game tally

letters.topic: A week of solitary hunting: two antelope and a deer

tr_quotes.text: Two field plover: shot with rifle, for pot.
I have been playing at frontier hunter in good earnest.

headline: Visitors crowd out the writing
summary: The Maltese Cross sits right on the main trail, so cowboys drop by every day to visit, and Roosevelt manages little writing.

events.detail: Passing cowboys stop daily to chat at the ranch house
Makes little progress on his writing

headline: Finding the Elkhorn site
summary: After a mallard for the pot, Roosevelt scouts the river north of Medora for a new ranch site. He buys a squatter's claim for $400, and a pair of locked elk antlers found on the ground gives the place its name: the Elkhorn.

events.detail: Shoots a mallard drake with a rifle for food
Searches north of Medora for a second ranch location
Pays a squatter $400 for his claim to the site
Names the new ranch Elkhorn after interlocked antlers found nearby

tr_quotes.text: One mallard drake, shot with rifle for pot.

headline: Turned away by Montana vigilantes
summary: Roosevelt travels by rail with the Marquis de Mores and a man named Jameson, to Mills City in Montana, hoping to join a vigilance group formed to stamp out horse stealing. The vigilantes turn all three down because they come from prominent families.

events.detail: Takes the train to Mills City with de Mores and Jameson
Seeks to join a vigilance committee against horse thieves; refused

headline: A pintail grouse for supper
summary: Back at the Maltese Cross, Roosevelt shoots a sharp-tailed grouse cock with his rifle for the table.

events.detail: Kills a pintail grouse with a rifle for food

tr_quotes.text: One cock pintail grouse, shot with rifle, for pot.

summary: Roosevelt is in New York as the Mandan Pioneer, back in Dakota, runs a piece on him and the reform fight in New York City politics.

headline: Democrats pick Cleveland and Hendricks
summary: The Democrats name New York's governor, Grover Cleveland, as their presidential candidate, with Thomas A. Hendricks as his running mate. Roosevelt loathes Hendricks as a Copperhead, a Northerner who sided with the South during the Civil War.

events.detail: Democratic convention nominates Cleveland and Hendricks

summary: Roosevelt stays on in Orange, New Jersey.

summary: Roosevelt takes his baby daughter Alice to Chestnut Hill to visit her mother's parents. Old college friends in Boston give him the cold shoulder, since many reform Republicans, the Mugwumps, have broken away to back Cleveland, along with a long list of major newspapers.

events.detail: Goes to Chestnut Hill with his daughter
Introduces the baby to her Lee grandparents
Snubbed in Boston by former Harvard companions
Mugwump reformers and many leading papers abandon Blaine for Cleveland

uncertain: Mugwump list gives surnames only for Godkin, Lowell and Dana; Lowell and Dana left as written.

events.detail: Goes to Lodge's summer home at Nahant
Evening conversation with Lodge on the porch

headline: Westward with Sewall and Dow
summary: Roosevelt meets Bill Sewall and Wilmot Dow in New York and the three set off for Medora. He tells Lodge that friends seem startled he has not sprouted hooves and horns.

Leaves with them for Medora
Jokes to Lodge about how his friends see him

letters.topic: Friends surprised he hasn't turned into a monster over Blaine

tr_quotes.text: Most of my friends seem surprised to find that I have not developed hooves and horns.

headline: An Englishman joins the party
summary: On the way to Dakota, Roosevelt, Sewall and Dow pick up a traveling companion at Harrisburg, an Englishman named Messiter, whom Roosevelt judges no great thinker but a gentleman.

events.detail: Traveling west by train

tr_quotes.text: an intellectual heavy weight,
gentleman

Founds the Elkhorn Ranch north of Medora with Sewall and Dow in charge
His herds total some 4,500 cattle, each ranch with its own brand

uncertain: This entry sums up the ranch setup rather than a dated event. The cowboys' nickname 'Maltee' comes from the record, and 'Ferris' is assumed to be Sylvane.

Merrifield and Ferris have delivered 1,000 head brought from Iowa

summary: Roosevelt spends the day after grouse near the Elkhorn.

headline: A tribute to Alice Lee

events.detail: Finishes a memorial tribute to Alice Hathaway Lee Roosevelt
Sends the manuscript to Putnam's for publication

tr_quotes.text: She was beautiful in face and form, and lovlier still in spirit; as a flower she grew, and as a fair young flower she died . . . and when my heart's dearest died, the light went from my life for ever.

works.title: Memorial tribute to Alice Hathaway Lee Roosevelt

headline: Fond of the grim Badlands
summary: At the Maltese Cross, Roosevelt writes of his growing affection for the stark Badlands landscape.

events.detail: Records his attachment to the Badlands

tr_quotes.text: I grow very fond of this place, and it certainly has a desolate, grim beauty of its own, that has a curious facination for me.

headline: Sombrero and a house under way
summary: Roosevelt writes Lodge that he would laugh to see him in his wide sombrero. To Bamie he recounts traveling out with his Maine friends and asks her to keep the builders moving on Leeholm, the new house she is overseeing at Oyster Bay.

events.detail: Writes Lodge about his cowboy look
Writes Bamie about the journey and the Leeholm construction

letters.topic: The trip west; prodding the Leeholm builders

tr_quotes.text: You would be amused to see me, in my broad sombrero hat.
stir Rich and Lorenzo up every now and then

uncertain: Rich and Lorenzo appear to be the Leeholm builders; full names not given.

headline: Facing down a gunman in Mingusville
summary: This is the likeliest date for Roosevelt's run-in at Nolan's Hotel in Mingusville. A drunk waving two pistols mocks him as a bespectacled dude; Roosevelt knocks him down, the shots go wild, and the man hits his head on the bar. The tale races across the Badlands.

events.detail: Puts up for the night at Nolan's Hotel, about 35 miles west of Medora
Floors an armed, drunken cowboy who singles him out; the man is hauled away

uncertain: Date is a historians' estimate; Hagedorn's Roosevelt in the Badlands places it in late June 1884.

headline: Backing a Tribune letter
summary: Roosevelt writes W. L. Hubbell confirming the facts in a Tribune letter concerning the state legislature.

events.detail: Writes Hubbell vouching for a Tribune letter on the New York Legislature

letters.topic: Confirms a Tribune letter about the Albany legislature

headline: On the Little Missouri
summary: Roosevelt is on the Little Missouri; no details are recorded.

events.detail: No activity recorded

headline: Outfitting for the Bighorns
summary: Roosevelt plans a two-month overland hunt to Wyoming's Bighorn Mountains with Bill Merrifield as hunting partner and a seasoned plainsman named Lebo as teamster and cook. His diary lists ponies, clothes, food and an arsenal of guns. That day he covers 72 miles in the saddle.

events.detail: Plans a long hunting expedition to the Bighorn Mountains
Itemizes his gear, ponies, provisions and firearms in his diary
Rides 72 miles from sunup to nightfall

tr_quotes.text: Have been spending a couple of weeks on my ranches, on the Little Missouri. I now intend starting out for two month's trip overland to the Bighorn Mountains.
My companions are my foreman, William Merrifield, who is to hunt with me, and an old french halfbreed named Lebo, who is to drive the team and to cook +c.
One of these is Blackie, a stout, swift rather vicious pony; Splitear, very enduring; Brownie, willing and swift, but very nervous; and Roachie, quiet and rather small.
Rode 72 miles between dawn and darkness

uncertain: The 72-mile ride comes from TR's August 17 letter to Bamie; the trip itself began August 18.

headline: A thousand-mile hunt ahead
summary: From Chimney Butte, Roosevelt tells Bamie about the coming hunting expedition and how much he has come to love the place.

events.detail: Writes Bamie about the planned trip

letters.topic: The upcoming expedition and his attachment to the ranch

tr_quotes.text: We will go in all nearly 1000 miles.
I grow very fond of this place.

headline: Hailstorm on the first day out
summary: The Bighorn trip gets a slow start. Roosevelt and Merrifield leave the wagon and ride to Lang's for the night, ducking into a washout when a hailstorm hits so hard the ponies won't face it. Their slickers keep them dry, and his new Winchester performs well.

events.detail: Sets out late on the expedition, leaving the wagon on the prairie
Shelters from a violent hailstorm in a washout
Spends the night at Gregor Lang's

tr_quotes.text: Made late start. Left wagon on prairie. Merrifield + I rode in and spent night at Langs. Out in prairie got caught in driving hail storm; sheltered in a wash out. Wind so strong could hardly stand; ponies would not face it.
The Winchester 45-75 shoots beautifully.

headline: Rain all day, roast duck at night
summary: In a steady downpour Roosevelt leaves Lang's, shoots ducks and grouse in the sloughs and skips lunch, then catches up with the wagon at Lake Station on the old Keogh Trail. They burn the old station's logs for a fire, eat fried duck and sleep in the wagon.

events.detail: Leaves Lang's after breakfast
Shoots 4 grouse and 5 young mallards with a rifle
Rejoins the wagon at Lake Station after dark

tr_quotes.text: Heavy rain storm all day.
Made fire of logs of old station house; good supper fried ducks.

headline: A whitetail buck in velvet
summary: Under gray skies the wagon struggles through soaked ground. Roosevelt drops a whitetail buck at a hundred yards and two sage grouse, all with his Winchester. They make only twelve miles and camp early at a muddy pool to dry out, crossing from prairie into rough Badlands.

events.detail: Kills a whitetail buck with velvet antlers and two sage grouse
Covers just 12 miles over heavy, wet ground
Makes camp by midafternoon to dry gear and water horses

tr_quotes.text: M. + I rode off; skirting some deep, branching brush bottomed coolies we spied a white tail buck feeding; I shot him through both shoulders at a hundred yards; good horns, but still in velvet.
Went through rolling prairies; and then in the abruptly broken and fantastically shaped Bad Lands.

headline: Cowboys singing to the herd
summary: After a frosty night, a big herd of beef steers that had bedded nearby passes the camp; all night Roosevelt heard the riders singing around it. The party's greyhound dies, and they make 25 miles past countless buffalo skulls. He sketches his companions Lebo and Merrifield in his diary.

events.detail: A herd of 1,500 steers and its cowboys pass the camp
The party's greyhound dies
Travels some 25 miles and camps near O'Fallon Creek's headwaters
Notes no live game but many old buffalo skulls and carcasses

tr_quotes.text: Early in morning a great herd of 1500 beef steers passed us; they had been bedded near us, and all night we had heard the cowboys singing and calling as they circled slowly round the herd.
Saw no living game; but hundreds of buffalo skulls and old carcasses.
Lebo is a chatty, tough old plainsman, full of expedients, and ready with both wits and hands. Merrifield is a good looking fellow, who shoots and rides beautifully; a reckless, self confident man.

uncertain: The diary's 'O'Fallow Creek' is read as O'Fallon Creek. Part of the line on how the dog died is hard to read in the record.

headline: Storm-soaked on the Keogh Trail
summary: A fierce night storm drenches the tentless party. Following a cattle trail southwest about twenty miles, Roosevelt misses two good shots at blacktail bucks. They camp beside a lovely natural park dotted with pine-topped sandstone pillars.

events.detail: A violent wind and rain storm soaks the camp overnight
Travels about 20 miles southwest along the Keogh Trail
Misses two shots at blacktail bucks in the foothills

tr_quotes.text: Camped for the night near a most beautiful natural park; green sward thickly dotted over with small, steep, isolated sand cliffs of most fantastic shap[e], crowned with pines.

headline: Cattle where buffalo once roamed
summary: The party crosses the Little Beaver onto wide brown-grass plains, where Roosevelt notes that cattle herds have replaced the buffalo. He misses a doe, shoots two young sage grouse through the head for the evening meal, and they camp in the Powder River Badlands to the howl of coyotes.

events.detail: Crosses Little Beaver Creek and rolls over open plains
Observes cattle ranges now filling former buffalo country
Misses a blacktail doe; kills two young sage grouse
Camps in the Powder River Badlands

tr_quotes.text: saw several herds of cattle, which have now taken the place of the buffalo, whose carcasses can be seen every where; this is already well occupied as a cattle country.
Coyotes howling.

headline: Letters written on a water keg
summary: The party follows a creek down to the Powder River and pushes on through sagebrush bottoms to a dry camp. Using an upturned keg as a desk, Roosevelt writes Bamie and Lodge and hands the letters to a passing cowboy. To Lodge he mixes trail news with talk of Cornwallis and the Puritans.

events.detail: Descends through the Powder River Badlands and travels up the river
Writes Bamie and Lodge on a water keg; a cowboy carries the mail

letters.topic: News from the trail on the Powder River
Daily travel, Lebo the cook, and thoughts on Cornwallis and the Puritans

tr_quotes.text: There are quite a number of cattle ranches along this river.
a character
I heartily enjoy this life.

headline: A pony tumbles down a cliff
summary: Moving up the Powder to where the Little Powder joins it, Roosevelt shoots grouse, doves and teal for the pot. Merrifield misses a cougar, the pair nearly bog down in a swamp, and Merrifield's pony somersaults twice down a thirty-foot sandy bank.

events.detail: Follows the Powder to its junction with the Little Powder
Kills 6 sharptail grouse, 2 doves and 2 teal with the shotgun
Unsuccessful whitetail hunt; Merrifield misses a cougar
Merrifield's pony tumbles down a steep sandy cliff
Sees beaver and whippoorwills

tr_quotes.text: M's pony turned two complete somersaults down a sandy cliff some thirty feet high. Saw beaver + whippoorwills.

headline: Night with the N Bar outfit
summary: A short day's travel. Roosevelt shoots eight prairie chickens and buys a fine young horse from a cowboy for $100. They stop at the N Bar Ranch, where thirty men and some three hundred horses are gearing up for the beef roundup, and he admires the cowboys' style.

events.detail: Shoots 8 sharptail grouse
Buys a young horse from a cowboy for $100
Stays at the N Bar Ranch as its crew prepares for the beef roundup

tr_quotes.text: Cowboys are a jolly set; picturesque, with broad hats, loosely knotted neckerchiefs, flannel shirts, leather chaparajos.

headline: A yearling buck in the swamp
summary: The Powder valley narrows between bold, pine-dotted bluffs. Roosevelt fills the bag with sage hens and prairie chickens, and at dusk, kneeling in a marsh, he shoots a young whitetail buck through the heart at fifty yards.

events.detail: Shoots sage hens and sharptail grouse with the shotgun
Kills a yearling whitetail buck from fifty yards

tr_quotes.text: Country prettier; bottoms narrower, hemmed in by bold bluffs, with pines scattered over them.

uncertain: The diary tally gives four whitetail bucks, probably a misreading of one.

headline: Nine crossings of the Powder
summary: Heading up the Powder, the party fords the river nine times, the wagon nearly sinking in quicksand once, and camps just short of Clear Creek.

events.detail: Fords the Powder nine times; wagon almost mired in quicksand
Camps near the mouth of Clear Creek

tr_quotes.text: Country very pretty.

headline: Two bucks with one bullet
summary: Climbing Clear Creek over barren sagebrush country, the wagon sticks three times and the team nearly gives out. In the afternoon Roosevelt breaks the backs of two blacktail bucks with a single shot at 431 paces and keeps the bullet.

events.detail: Hauls the wagon through washouts with ropes tied to the saddle horses
Kills two blacktail bucks with one long rifle shot

tr_quotes.text: two stood side by side; taking careful aim I broke the backs of both with one bullet; distance 431 paces (near 400 yards) actual walking. Best shot I ever made. Kept bullet.

headline: Into Wyoming
summary: The party makes about twenty miles up Clear Creek and crosses from Montana into Wyoming, passing many cattle and a Cheyenne camp. Roosevelt notes that he has been bathing in the river daily.

events.detail: Travels some 20 miles and crosses into Wyoming Territory
Passes a Cheyenne encampment

tr_quotes.text: Have had a bath in the river every day lately.

headline: Bighorns in sight, marksmanship match
summary: Camped a few miles from Buffalo with the snowy Bighorns in view, Roosevelt nearly halves a jackrabbit at 75 yards. Near a Cheyenne village, Merrifield proposes a shooting match, and the two hunters easily beat the Cheyenne marksmen.

events.detail: Continues up Clear Creek; camps outside Buffalo
Shoots a jackrabbit at about 75 yards
Wins a shooting contest against Cheyenne men

tr_quotes.text: Have for last three days been in sight of the snow streaked Bighorn Mts.
Nowhere, not even at sea, does a man feel more lonely than when riding over the far-reaching, seemingly never-ending plains.

headline: Rolling into Buffalo, Wyoming
summary: The hunting party reaches Buffalo, which Roosevelt sizes up as a genuine frontier settlement.

events.detail: Arrives at Buffalo, Wyoming Territory

tr_quotes.text: Reached Buffalo, Wyoming, quite a frontier town.

headline: Trading the wagon for pack ponies
summary: At a Crazy Woman Creek sawmill the party leaves its wagon behind and sets up a pack string of seven horses, with the wagon cover doubling as a tent, for the climb into the mountains.

events.detail: Arrives at a sawmill on Crazy Woman Creek
Repacks for the mountains: three saddle horses, three pack animals and a spare

tr_quotes.text: Here we leave our wagon and go in on pack ponies. Have seven horses, 3 to ride, 3 to pack, 1 spare.

headline: Up onto the Bighorn plateau
summary: Balky ponies and a faint trail delay the start until ten. The party grinds up the steep climb to the Bighorn plateau, camps on Willow Creek, and Roosevelt shoots two blue grouse out of a tree for supper. Ice forms overnight.

events.detail: Climbs to the Bighorn plateau with the pack string
Camps on Willow Creek in the cold
Shoots two blue grouse with the rifle

tr_quotes.text: Camped on willow creek. Already pretty cold.
Ascent to the Bighorn Plateau was very steep. Ice formed at night.

headline: First elk in the high country
summary: The party works up to about 8,000 feet into green park country of glades, lakes and clear streams and camps by a rushing creek. Hunting on foot, Roosevelt trails a band of elk and kills a cow and a calf; Merrifield takes two more.

events.detail: Advances about six miles to a camp by a mountain stream
Tracks an elk herd on foot and kills two; Merrifield kills two

tr_quotes.text: I found fresh tracks of a band of elk, and followed them up till I came on them; killed an old cow and a bull calf as they ran off through the woods, M afterwords killed two.

headline: Chasing a bugling bull
summary: With the ponies worn out, they stay put to dry meat and stretch hides. A bull elk calling near camp the night before lures Roosevelt out alone all day, but he never sees it, coming home with only a rabbit and a grouse.

events.detail: Rest day to dry meat and stretch hides
Spends the day tracking a bull elk on foot without success
Shoots a rabbit and a blue grouse

tr_quotes.text: An old bull elk, whistling and calling, almost came in to camp last night; today I went off alone on foot to trail him up; was absent all day but never saw him

headline: Snowbound beside the fire
summary: Snow covers the camp by morning and rain and sleet fall all day, so the men stay in the tent before a roaring log fire. In the afternoon Roosevelt takes a brisk three-hour ride on his horse California through the mist.

events.detail: Snow, rain and sleet keep the party in camp
Rides California for three hours in the rain

tr_quotes.text: Stormed all night; when we waked up snow covered the ground, bending down the willow bushes and loading the tall pines

uncertain: The diary passage is cut off in the record.

headline: Helter-skelter after three bulls
summary: Roosevelt and Merrifield ride out at dawn on Blackie and Splitear and hunt until dusk over rough burned timber. They find three bull elk and wound all of them, give chase on foot, and bring down two; Roosevelt also kills a blacktail doe. He is fascinated by the bulls' bugling in the rut.

events.detail: Pursues three wounded bull elk on foot and kills two
Kills a blacktail doe
Observes elk bugling and behavior during the mating season

tr_quotes.text: we found three bulls; we wounded all three (I two + M. one) and went after them helter skelter, running, tumbling, jumping, falling and shooting.

headline: Merrifield trees a black bear
summary: Out alone, Roosevelt lets a doe and two fawns pass since camp has plenty of meat, then shoots a dozen blue grouse for variety. Meanwhile Merrifield chases a black bear up a tree and kills it, to Roosevelt's regret at missing it.

events.detail: Spares a doe and fawns; kills 12 blue grouse
Merrifield runs a black bear up a tree and shoots it

tr_quotes.text: I rode out alone; saw a doe and two fawns, which I did not touch, as we have more than enough meat
Meanwhile M, ran a black bear up a tree and shot him; by bad luck I was not with him.

headline: Snow, moonlight and bear meat
summary: The party moves camp about six miles to a fork of the Ten Sleep. Snow falls off and on, and Roosevelt finds the scene lovely by moonlight. He reports the bear meat tasty and his health never better.

events.detail: Shifts camp to a branch of Ten Sleep Creek

tr_quotes.text: in the moonlight at night the scenery is very beautiful.
The bear meat is very good eating; I have never been in better health.

headline: Woods that recall Maine
summary: A long, fruitless still-hunt with Merrifield turns up only a few deer tracks amid snow and frozen ponds. The silent pine and spruce forest reminds Roosevelt of the woods of Maine and the Adirondacks.

events.detail: Still-hunts through snowy woods without seeing game
Reflects on the mountain forests' sights and silences

tr_quotes.text: These pine and spruce forests with their sights + sounds or more often, absence of sound, remind me of the great woods of Maine and the Adirondacs [sic]; they have a weird, melancholy facination for me.

headline: Fifty trout and a weary hike
summary: Roosevelt and Merrifield ride and hike most of the day to reach a mountain lake, catch about fifty trout, and return exhausted to a trout feast in camp.

events.detail: Fishes a mountain lake and catches some fifty trout
Four hours riding and six of tough walking

tr_quotes.text: Pretty tired, and glad to get back to camp and a first class trout supper.

headline: A great bull elk at 75 yards
summary: Finding no game, they move camp six miles toward the foothills. Hunting on foot that afternoon, Roosevelt kills a big bull elk with a superb rack facing him at 75 yards, and picks off two grouse for supper.

events.detail: Moves camp lower into a narrow wooded valley
Kills a large bull elk with a single shot
Shoots two grouse

tr_quotes.text: I got a shot 'at a great bull elk with magnificent antlers as he stood facing me 75 yards (81 paces off, [sic] killing him very neatly.

headline: His first grizzly
summary: Roosevelt shoots a spike blacktail in the morning, wearing moccasins for silence. That afternoon he and Merrifield trail a grizzly through thick forest to its bed, and Roosevelt kills it with one shot to the brain from 25 feet. He is very proud of his first bear.

events.detail: Kills a young blacktail buck at forty yards
Tracks a grizzly to its bed and kills it at close range

tr_quotes.text: found a grizzly bear track in a dense forest; followed the trail noiselessly up, and found him in his bed; I shot him through the brain at 25 feet distance.
I was very proud over my first bear.

uncertain: The size figures in the record (9 feet, 1,200 lbs.) are not TR's diary words and are left out.

headline: A sow grizzly and her cub
summary: After skinning yesterday's grizzly, Roosevelt rides to a scenic canyon and needs six shots to kill a blacktail buck. While skinning it at dusk, he and Merrifield spot a mother grizzly and a big cub, chase them a mile on foot, and kill both.

events.detail: Skins the grizzly from the day before
Kills a blacktail buck after a run of poor shooting
Runs down and kills a female grizzly and her cub with Merrifield

tr_quotes.text: Down to canyon; superb scenery.
I mortally wounded the old one; she turned to bay and M, who was ahead, finished her

headline: A grizzly for Merrifield
summary: The men haul the bears into camp. That afternoon they find a big grizzly feeding on the bull elk carcass, and Roosevelt has Merrifield take the shot, since he has yet to kill one on his own. Four blue grouse make supper.

events.detail: Brings the dead bears in to camp
Lets Merrifield shoot a grizzly found at the elk carcass
Shoots four blue grouse

tr_quotes.text: M. has not yet got one solely his own gun; so I made him shoot it.

headline: An elk on the run
summary: All three men beat the woods for bear all day with no luck. When Lebo misses a bull elk, it crosses Roosevelt's path; he wounds it, sprints after it in his moccasins, and drops it with a second shot.

events.detail: Daylong bear drive on foot, no bears seen
Kills a bull elk that Lebo had missed

tr_quotes.text: running at top speed in my light moccasins, I got another shot and broke his back.

headline: Leaving the mountains
summary: The party breaks camp and starts down, three pack ponies loaded with hides and antlers, and camps again on the creek they used coming up.

events.detail: Breaks camp and heads down the mountain with loaded pack ponies
Camps on the way down

tr_quotes.text: Broke camp and started off the mountain. Three pack ponies heavily laden with hides and horns

uncertain: Diary 'Willow Oak' likely means Willow Creek, used on the way up.

headline: Back to the wagon
summary: The party reaches the Crazy Woman Creek sawmill where the wagon waited. Roosevelt's horse California is worn out after falling into a creek.

events.detail: Returns to the sawmill and the wagon
California tumbles into a creek and is exhausted

tr_quotes.text: California all done up, having fallen into a creek.

headline: Dinner at Fort McKinney
summary: With the wagon back in service, the party rolls to Fort McKinney, where Roosevelt dines at the post. He jots down a Dr. Tyrell's account of two 8th Cavalry soldiers killed by a grizzly in New Mexico in 1872.

events.detail: Travels by wagon to Fort McKinney
Dines with the officers at the fort

tr_quotes.text: Went (with wagon again) to Fort McKinney. Dined at Fort.

uncertain: Dr. Tyrell's role is inferred from the diary note; the spelling follows the record.

headline: Starting the 300-mile trip home
summary: The party makes a decent day's travel, camping above Piney Fork, and Roosevelt bags a jackrabbit and two ducks. He writes Bamie about his bears and elk as they head home.

events.detail: Begins the long return journey; camps above Piney Fork
Shoots a jackrabbit and two ducks
Writes Bamie about his bear and elk

letters.topic: His bear and elk kills; the homeward trek begins

tr_quotes.text: Fair days Journey. Camped above Piney Fork.

headline: Camp under the balm tree
summary: A long day on the trail brings the party back to its August 30 lunch spot beneath a big balm tree, where they camp.

events.detail: Long march; camps at an earlier stopping place

tr_quotes.text: Camped where we lunched on Aug 30th; under a great Balm Tree.

headline: Saving the bear skins
summary: The party follows Clear Creek to within six miles of the Powder, then stops under two big cottonwoods so the spoiling bear hides can be scraped and dried. The horses are in poor shape.

events.detail: Descends Clear Creek and makes camp
Halts to flesh and dry the bear hides

tr_quotes.text: Horses are not in good condition.

headline: Waiting on the hides
summary: The bear skins are still drying, so the party stays put. Roosevelt hunts the north side of the creek and sees nothing.

events.detail: Hunts north of the creek without success

tr_quotes.text: Bear skins drying, so did not break camp; hunted to north of creek; no game.

headline: Teal and chickens by the river
summary: With the hides still damp, Roosevelt hunts south of the creek without luck, then takes the shotgun along the river and bags two teal and five sharptail grouse.

events.detail: Fruitless hunt south of the creek
Shoots 2 teal and 5 sharptail grouse along the river

tr_quotes.text: Skins not yet dry; hunted to south side of creek; no game

headline: An off day with the rifle
summary: After a long day's travel the party camps where the Powder curves. Short of fresh meat, Roosevelt goes hunting but misses three whitetail shots, and Merrifield misses two.

events.detail: Long day's journey; camps among cottonwoods on the Powder
Misses several whitetail shots; Merrifield also misses

tr_quotes.text: Out of fresh meat, so went out shooting; shot awfully

headline: Wet night, whitetail doe
summary: Rain soaks the men overnight despite the wagon cover. They travel well and camp a few miles upriver from the N Bar Ranch, and Merrifield brings down a whitetail doe.

events.detail: Good day's travel; camps near the N Bar Ranch
Merrifield kills a whitetail doe

tr_quotes.text: Rained all night; drew wagon sheet over us, but pretty wet.

headline: Camp by the S H ranch
summary: The party pastures its horses near the S H ranch, and it rains again overnight. Back East, Roosevelt's sister Corinne turns 23.

events.detail: Stops to graze the horses at the S H ranch
Corinne's 23rd birthday

tr_quotes.text: Made pasture by S H ranche. Rained at night.

headline: A dozen ducks near Powderville
summary: Traveling down the Powder, the party camps near Powderville. Roosevelt shoots two blue-winged teal with the rifle and ten more ducks with a right-and-left from the shotgun.

events.detail: Heads down the Powder and camps near Powderville
Kills 12 ducks

tr_quotes.text: Shot two bluewinged teal with rifle, and eight teal and two shovellers with a right and left from shot gun.

headline: Cold rain and muddy water
summary: Cold rain falls through the night and all the next day. The party travels until dark and camps near White Clay Buttes with poor grass and muddy water, the team nearly spent.

events.detail: Travels in steady cold rain; camps at White Clay Buttes

tr_quotes.text: water bad, from mud hole; team nearly done out.

headline: Pitch-pine fire at the Medicine Buttes
summary: After a hard frost, Roosevelt shoots seven sharptail grouse. On a cold, windy day one team horse gives out and Splitear goes into harness. They camp after dark among the Medicine Buttes beside a blazing pitch-pine fire under a sandstone cliff.

events.detail: Shoots 7 sharptail grouse
Hard day's travel; pony Splitear replaces a played-out team horse
Camps among the Medicine Buttes after nightfall

tr_quotes.text: It was after dark when we went in to camp among the fantastic 'medicine buttes'; a most picturesque camp, blazing pitch pine fire, is angle of a sand stone cliff, under pine trees.
